en: When
building AI agents or AI workflows, or
actually when writing any kind of program,
you can of course write the code you want.
You can follow patterns you want. You can
use design approaches you prefer.
What you'll often see when working with AI
agents though
is that classes are being used, that
object-oriented principles are being used,
at least to some extent, which is why I
migrated this example from before, which was
only using functions, which again is fine,
but I still migrated it to a class-based
approach to also show you how that could
look like in case you're interested in that.
And for that, of course, attached you find
an updated main.py file.
The database.py file did not change, but in
the main.py file, I defined a tool class and
we'll take a look at it in a second and then
some specialized tool classes that extend
this base tool class and we'll dive into
those in a second too.
And you already might guess it, I defined an
agent class, a base class and then also a
specialized agent class for this customer
service agent.
And the idea behind this class-based
approach here of course is
that you could easily add multiple tools or
multiple agents and build up on those base
classes so that you don't have to
reimplement all the logic over and over
again.
And it's of course up to you how much logic
you wanna shift into the base class and how
much logic you wanna keep specific to a
certain tool or agent.
Now let's start with the tool base class.
Let's start with exploring that and how such
a class could look like.
And here I decided that a tool in the end is
just a function. So it should have a name,
it should have a description, which is
important for the AI
model, for the large language model to
evaluate whether a certain tool should be
used or not.
And it will have parameters.
